core_summary: This chapter explores essential biological functions required to maintain life: nutrition, respiration, transportation, and excretion. It compares autotrophic photosynthesis in plants with heterotrophic digestion in organisms ranging from unicellular Amoeba to human beings. It details aerobic and anaerobic respiratory pathways of glucose breakdown, circulatory mechanisms involving the human four-chambered heart and plant vascular transport (xylem and phloem), and excretory filtration by nephrons in human kidneys alongside plant waste management.
key_concepts: Definition of life processes maintaining cellular order and preventing somatic breakdown
Autotrophic nutrition: Light-dependent conversion of CO2 and H2O into glucose and starch via chlorophyll and stomatal gas exchange
Heterotrophic nutrition strategies: Holozoic (Amoeba, humans), Saprophytic (fungi), and Parasitic (cuscuta, ticks)
Human digestive system: Mechanical crushing, enzymatic breakdown (salivary amylase, pepsin, trypsin, lipase), emulsification by bile, and intestinal villi absorption
Breakdown pathways of 6-carbon glucose into 3-carbon pyruvate, yielding ATP aerobically (mitochondria) or anaerobically (yeast fermentation, human muscle lactic acid build-up)
Human respiratory system: Nasal cilia filtering, tracheal rings of cartilage, and alveolar capillary gas exchange

Human circulatory system: Double circulation through a 4-chambered heart separating oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, blood pressure, and vascular system (arteries, veins, capillaries, platelets, lymph)
Plant transport: Transpiration pull and root pressure moving water/minerals through xylem; translocation of sucrose via phloem requiring ATP energy
Human excretory system: Renal blood filtration through nephrons (glomerular filtration, selective reabsorption, tubular secretion) and urine accumulation in bladder
Excretory strategies in plants: Gaseous release via stomata, leaf abscission, resin/gum storage in old xylem, and root excretion into soil

key_terms.definition: The basic essential maintenance activities performed by living organisms to sustain life.
Mode of nutrition where organisms synthesise their own organic food from simple inorganic raw materials using light energy.
The process by which green plants convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll.
Microscopic pores on leaf surfaces guarded by guard cells, facilitating gas exchange and transpiration.
Biological catalysts that accelerate chemical reactions and nutrient digestion in living organisms.
Rhythmic wave-like muscular contractions of the alimentary canal lining that push food forward.
The breakdown of large fat globules into smaller droplets by bile salts to increase lipase action efficiency.
Finger-like projections on the inner mucosal lining of the small intestine that greatly expand surface area for nutrient absorption.
The cellular energy currency generated during respiration that fuels cellular metabolic activities.
Breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen inside mitochondria, producing CO2, water, and large ATP yield.
Breakdown of glucose in the absence of oxygen in cell cytoplasm, producing ethanol/lactic acid and low ATP yield.
Tiny balloon-like vascularized air sacs in lungs providing maximal surface area for respiratory gas exchange.
A circulatory pattern where blood passes through the heart twice during one complete cycle through the body (pulmonary and systemic loops).
The loss of water vapor from aerial parts of a plant, primarily through stomata, generating suction pull for xylem transport.
The active transport of soluble photosynthetic products (like sucrose) through phloem tissue.
The basic structural and functional microscopic filtering unit of the kidney.

key_takeaways: Unicellular organisms rely on simple diffusion for gas and waste transport, whereas multicellular organisms require dedicated organ systems.
Anaerobic respiration in human skeletal muscles during vigorous exercise produces lactic acid, causing localized muscle cramps.
Four-chambered hearts in birds and mammals prevent mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, supporting high metabolic temperature regulation.
Xylem transport of water is driven passively by transpiration pull and osmotic root pressure, while phloem translocation of food requires active energy expenditure via ATP.
Kidneys maintain osmotic and fluid balance by filtering metabolic nitrogenous wastes (urea/uric acid) from blood while selectively reabsorbing glucose, amino acids, salts, and water.
